threads.author: threeway_02
threads.title: 36 and switching to electrical: union apprenticeship, trade school, or just find a shop?
threads.body:
I'm 36, been in insurance claims for 11 years and I'm done with it. I want to get into electrical. I've read a lot and I keep going in circles on the three options:

1. Apply to the IBEW apprenticeship (I'm in Irvington, so I think that's 102?)
2. Do a night program somewhere first
3. Just call shops and try to get hired as a helper

I have some savings but not a ton. Which of these actually gets me working and learning soonest? I'd appreciate honest answers, including "you're too late for X" if that's the case.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Not too late for any of them. We've had first-years in their late 30s and they tend to be the ones who show up.

On the union side: I can't give you dates, the application window and the aptitude test schedule are posted by the apprenticeship itself, so go to their site or call and ask. When I applied it was an aptitude test (math and reading), then an interview, then a ranked list. Could be different now. Irvington, I'd check whether you fall under 102 or another local before you apply; jurisdiction lines are not always where you'd guess.

While you wait, get hired by a shop. Hours on a job never hurt an application. Stay safe.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body:
Honestly I'd do 2 and 3 at the same time. Night school while you work as a helper. The list can take a while and you're 36, you want to be earning something now.

I went the trade school route and got hired faster than any of my buddies on the list. That was me though, and it was a long time ago. Your mileage may vary.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: 4th year in 164. applied at 24, got in the second time I took the test. worth it for me... but go work somewhere while you wait, the guys who come in with some hours are way ahead day one

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Different trade but same question I get from every kid who walks in my shop. I was in the union a few years before I came back to my father's business. The school and the benefits were the best part and I won't pretend otherwise. My father used to say the union teaches you the trade and a good shop teaches you the customer. You want both eventually.

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body:
This is really helpful, thank you. Sounds like the answer is "apply, and get a helper job now regardless."

edit: thanks everyone. Called two shops today, one wants me to come in Monday.

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: 40 and haven't even picked a trade yet. Am I kidding myself?
threads.body:
So I'm 40, Piscataway, been managing a call center for a long time. I like working with my hands, I fix everything at home, and I'm tired of spreadsheets about other people's work.

Problem is I can't decide between electrical, HVAC, and plumbing, and every week I change my mind. Also the money: I make decent now and I know the first year or two is a big cut. And my knees aren't 20 anymore.

For anyone who switched later in life, how did you decide, and how bad was the first year really?

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Pay-cut math I'd do before deciding:
- Your take-home now vs a helper's hourly rate times realistic hours (not 60/week, assume 45)
- Months of savings that covers the gap for 2 years, not 1
- Whether the shop pays for school, tools, a van, overtime
- Health insurance: who covers it and what it costs you

If the numbers work for 2 years, the age part is the easy part.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, for what it's worth: shows up on time, listens, doesn't need to be told twice. Age isn't on that list. Some of my best guys started in their 30s and 40s.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: Appreciate all of this. Kash, the two-year math is the part I hadn't actually done. Going to run real numbers, and ask around about seeing each trade up close before the end of the year.

threads.author: ms_almonte
threads.title: EPA 608: what my students get wrong every year
threads.body:
Every fall somebody in my class assumes the 608 is a formality. Here's what actually trips people up, in order.

First, they skip the Core section because it "isn't technical." Core is where people fail. It's rules, dates, recovery requirements, and it's all memorization.

Second, they cram the night before. You need to know the rules, not just recognize answers.

Third, they don't ask how their specific test is given. The format depends on which type and who's proctoring it, so ask the testing organization before you show up.

Go for Universal if you can. Ask me how I know you'll want it later.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Universal is realistic if you study, even with zero background. Plenty of my 17-year-olds pass it. Do the practice tests until Core is boring.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... I had a guy on my crew who failed Core three times because he kept saying it was common sense lol. It isn't. Study the dates.

threads.author: LiveFrontLessons
threads.title: failed rough-in, boss says the inspector is wrong. who do i believe
threads.body:
1st year out of vo-tech, working for a small shop near asbury. we failed a rough in on a bathroom remodel today. inspector wrote up "physical protection" on a couple runs where the cable goes through studs, and something about the box by the vanity being too full.

boss says the inspector is being picky and he's done it this way for years. i don't want to say anything dumb but i also want to understand it. who's right

edit: it was nail plates on two studs where the holes were close to the edge. boss fixed it, passed on reinspection. thanks for explaining instead of just dunking on me

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it. When cable runs through a hole close to the edge of a stud, it needs protection so a drywall screw doesn't find it. That's what a nail plate is for, and it's one of the most common write-ups I see. Box fill is counting conductors, devices and clamps against the box's volume; a small box with a GFCI and a couple of cables fills up fast.

The inspector is enforcing whatever code edition is in effect for that permit. Next time, ask politely for the section number. Most inspectors will give it to you and respect you more for asking.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly nail plates are the number one thing I see guys skip on remodels down here. Your boss knows better, he just didn't want to hear it in front of you.

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: your boss is wrong lol. 9 times out of 10 when somebody says the inspector is picky, it's nail plates

replies.author: LiveFrontLessons
replies.body: thanks both. going to buy my own box of nail plates so it's never my fault again

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: What should a 2nd-year non-union plumber make in Central Jersey?
threads.body:
Two years in at a non-union shop near Manville. Service and some remodel work. I'm at $21/hr, no overtime most weeks, I drive my own car to jobs. A guy I went to school with says I'm getting robbed, another says that's normal.

Not trying to start a fight, just want to know if I should ask for a raise and what's reasonable to ask for.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Rates swing a lot by shop and trade, so look at the whole package, not just the hourly:
- Do they pay for school or your license prep?
- Overtime: how often, and is it paid at time and a half?
- Mileage or a van: you driving your own car is a real cost
- Health insurance, PTO, tools

$21 with your own car and no benefits is on the low side for 2 years in, from what I see around here. Ask for a review, come with what you've learned to do on your own.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Careful with whatever number your school friend is comparing you to. If he's heard of a 2nd-year non-union helper making $40 an hour in Central Jersey, that isn't typical. Either that guy's in the union and you're hearing the total package, or he's on a prevailing-wage job, or it's a story. Comparing a cash rate to a union package isn't apples to apples.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: He's right. The locals usually publish their wage and benefit package, so look that up on the local's site if you want a real comparison, and remember the benefits are a big piece of the number.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Thanks. Going to ask for a review next month and bring up mileage. Will report back.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Before you go out on your own: what nobody tells you about year one
threads.body:
I get asked about this every week, so here's my list from 25 years, the last 14 running my own company:
- Get your license first. As I understand NJ's rules, registering as a home improvement contractor is not the same as holding a trade license, and it doesn't let you do licensed work. Check with Consumer Affairs.
- Insurance will cost more than you think, and you need it before your first job, not after.
- Price for callbacks. If you don't, every callback comes out of your pocket.
- Your first truck doesn't need to be new. It needs to start every morning in January.
- Keep your books from day one, or pay someone who will.
- Most new owners undercharge for the first two years. I did.

Ask questions below, I'll answer what I can.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: I'd add: decide early whether you want public work. Prevailing-wage jobs mean certified payroll and a lot of paperwork, at least on every one we've done. Good money, different business.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: And if you're taking over a family shop instead of starting one, it's all the same plus your father second-guessing every price you quote. Ask me how that's going.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
On the first point, since it comes up every time, the short answer as I understand it:
- Home improvement registration is for general home improvement work
- HVACR work needs the HVACR license (or working under someone who has it)
- Check with Consumer Affairs for your situation; don't take a contractor's word for legal stuff, including mine

threads.author: Exit117Plumber
threads.title: Why did my sweat joint leak? Should I just learn press?
threads.body: Vo-tech senior, helping my uncle on weekends. Sweated a 3/4 tee on Saturday, cleaned it, fluxed it, looked perfect. Turned the water on and it dripped. Redid it and it dripped again. Uncle says just buy a press tool and stop wasting solder lol. Is sweating even worth learning anymore?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Learn to sweat, kid. Press is great and I own the tools, but you'll be on jobs where you can't press, and you need to know why joints fail.

Nine out of ten times a joint that looks perfect and drips has water in the line. Water in the pipe pulls the heat away and the solder never flows all the way in. Was there a valve or a low spot near that tee?

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Agree with Ziggy. And heat the fitting, not the solder. When the solder gets pulled in on its own, you're there.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: There was a valve about a foot away that was weeping a little. So yeah, probably water.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: There's your water. Fix the valve or get the water out first, then sweat it. You'll never forget this one.

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: Two years non-union in Somerset. Too late to try for the UA apprenticeship?
threads.body:
Sorry if this has been asked a hundred times. I posted a while back about making $21 an hour near Manville. I did ask for the review. I got fifty cents and a "we'll see in the spring."

I like the work and the guys, but I keep thinking about the union apprenticeship. I'm two years in. Would I be starting over at zero? Is there any credit for time already worked, or do they not care? I'd also be risking a paycheck I count on for something I might not get.

Not trying to trash my shop, they've been fair in other ways. I just want to know if this is a smart move or a step backward.
fact_risk: whether UA programs credit prior non-union experience
UA Local 9 covers the Manville area
application periods

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Not a step backward. Different trade from mine, so take this as general.

Time you've already worked counts for something in the interview, because you can talk about real jobs. Whether it shortens the apprenticeship itself is a question for that program, not for me. Some programs have a way to evaluate prior experience and some don't, and those rules change.

What I'd do: apply while you keep the paycheck. Filling out an application doesn't require quitting anything. If you get called, then you decide. Stay safe.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body:
I'll give you the other side. I went union for a few years and then came back to my father's shop. The benefits were real and the school was better than anything I got on the job. What I didn't like was having no say in where I went.

My father used to say a man who takes the first offer never learns what he's worth. Ask the union your questions, ask your shop what their plan for you is, then compare.

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: brother you're 2 years in and they gave you 50 cents. apply. worst case they say no and you still have the job

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly 50 cents after two years would bug me too. But don't hear 'we'll see' as a no, small shops get squeezed in the fall. Ask him straight what you'd need to show by spring to get a real bump. If he can't answer, that's your answer.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, from the other side of the table: someone two years in who can explain what they did on a job, start to finish. That's worth more than a certificate. Union or not, keep a record of your work with dates and who supervised you. Whoever you talk to next will ask.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, the guys who regret it are the ones who never applied. A form costs you nothing. Keep showing up to the shop until somebody hands you something better. That's the job.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body:
Thank you all, this is more than I expected. I'm going to call Local 9 this week and ask how prior experience works before I do anything else.

edit: called and left a message, waiting on a callback. Started writing down my last two years of jobs from my phone calendar in the meantime.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: My shop teacher won't stop pushing the union application. Why is he so sure?
threads.body:
Some context first because it matters. I'm in the electrical program at the Mercer County vo-tech, I've been doing weekend helper stuff for a guy in Hamilton since June (mostly carrying, some pulling wire), and my shop teacher brings up the IBEW application basically every class. Like every single class. He hands out the flyer, he talks about the pension, he tells us non-union is a dead end.

The guy I work weekends for is non-union and he's doing fine. Owns two vans, takes his family to Wildwood every August.

So who's right? I'm not against the union. I just don't like being told there's one answer when I can see with my own eyes there's at least two.
fact_risk: union apprenticeship features (wage scale, benefits, school)
IBEW Local 400 jurisdiction for Manahawkin

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Your teacher has probably watched what the apprenticeship did for students before you, and that's a fair reason to push it. Structured school, a wage scale that steps up on a schedule, benefits, safety training built in. Those are real.

"Dead end" is too strong, though. Plenty of non-union electricians do well, and your weekend guy is proof. The honest version: the union path is a known path, and a good non-union shop can also be a good path. Apply, keep working weekends, and decide with real offers in front of you. Stay safe.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'm the non-union guy your teacher is warning you about. Own my shop in Long Branch, went to trade school, did fine. But I'll admit the union guys my age have a pension I don't. Both things are true. Don't let either side tell you the other one's a scam.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body:
> Don't let either side tell you the other one's a scam

Fair. I didn't mean my teacher's scamming anybody. It's the "dead end" thing that gets me, because my weekend guy clearly isn't one.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: I left the union and I half regret it, so take that for what it is. What I miss most is the training. What I don't miss is sitting by the phone between jobs some years. My father used to say every road has tolls, you just have to know which ones you're paying.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire a kid out of vo-tech: shows up, has some hours, can pass a background check. Whether he applied to the union doesn't come into it. If you end up non-union, ask about school and how raises work before you take the job.

threads.title: To the kids who ranked low this summer
threads.body:
Saw a few of you beating yourselves up over a number. Here's what I tell my own helpers.

A ranking is one morning of your life. It doesn't know whether you show up, whether you listen, or whether you can carry a 50-gallon heater up a split-level's stairs without banging the drywall.

Go get a job with somebody who'll teach you. Learn to solder, learn to read a boiler, learn to talk to a homeowner without making her nervous. Then apply again with something to say. I've hired plenty of kids who never got into anything, and they're running service calls on their own now.

Don't quit on it. That's the job.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Before you sign a private trade school loan, ask these questions
threads.body:
Every few weeks a new hire tells me what they owe on a private trade school program, and some of them didn't need to owe it. I'm not against private schools. Some are good. But ask these before you sign anything:
- What's the total cost, including tools, books and fees, not the monthly payment
- How many hours are hands-on shop time versus classroom
- What share of graduates are working in the trade a year later, and how do they count that
- Does the county vo-tech or community college near you have an adult program for less
- Would an employer pay for it if you got hired first

If the admissions person gets pushy when you ask, that's an answer too.
fact_risk: private school vs county adult program cost difference

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: All good questions. I'd add one from my side: ask to sit in on a shop class before you enroll, on a normal night. You'll see in ten minutes whether students are working or watching. Ask me how I know some programs don't love that request.

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Update: did a ride-along in all three trades. Here's what happened
threads.body:
A while back I posted about being 40 and unable to pick a trade. Kash has been mentoring me since then, and he helped me line up a ride-along in each trade, so here's the report.

Plumbing: a day on a repipe in an old Colonial in Metuchen. Loved the problem-solving, hated my knees by 2pm.
HVAC: a changeout in a split-level in Edison in August. The attic was brutal, but the diagnosis part was interesting.
Electrical: a service upgrade in Highland Park, panel swap, PSE&G had to come out to pull the meter. That was the one where I lost track of time.

So I'm leaning electrical, and maybe the low-voltage side later because of my knees. Two questions: did anyone else pick partly because of their body? And is it crazy to plan around knees at 40?

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Planning around your body at 40 isn't crazy, it's smart. When I hire someone in their 40s, the ones I keep know their limits and tell me up front. That's worth more to me than someone who says yes to every attic and gets hurt in a month.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: As a vo-tech kid who thinks about this way too much: a panel swap was the best day of my whole summer too, and the meter pull part is wild the first time you see it.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Good process. If you go electrical and later want low voltage:
- Get your OSHA 10 early
- Ask every shop you interview with whether they do any controls or fire alarm work
- Keep notes on every panel and service you touch

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Love this. One thing my older students tell me: the first year is harder on the body than any year after, because you're doing everything the slow way. It gets easier as you get efficient. So don't judge your knees by one day on a repipe.

threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: From the inspection side: whose license belongs on a heat pump swap
threads.body:
I get some version of this question every week this time of year, so I'll put it in one place. Not legal advice; your local construction office has the final word.

As I understand the current rules, a condenser or heat pump replacement in NJ usually touches more than one subcode. The mechanical work goes on a permit from a contractor holding the HVACR license. The new disconnect, the whip and any circuit changes are electrical work, which means an Electrical Contractor pulls that permit or the work is done under one. Some companies have both licenses in-house. Plenty don't, and that's where I see trouble: the HVAC crew runs a new circuit because the panel was right there, and nobody pulled the electrical.

The HVACR license is also newer than a lot of people assume. If I remember right it became required around 2014, so you'll still meet techs who talk like it doesn't exist.

If you're a helper and you don't know whose license a job is under, it's a fair thing to ask. And find out which edition of the code the permit falls under; it changes what I look for.

Saw this twice this summer on fit-outs, so I'm posting it for the electrical apprentices.

You're demoing a space, there's an old split system or a rooftop unit coming out, and someone hands a first-year a pair of cutters and points at the copper. Don't. Ask the GC or the HVAC sub, "has this been recovered?" and get a name. It's the same as LOTO: you don't assume it's dead because somebody said it probably is. Glasses and gloves either way. Stay safe.

threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: Inspectors notice which helpers are paying attention
threads.body:
Something I've noticed from the inspection side, for anyone stuck in the material-and-cleanup months.

The helpers who come along on inspections and actually listen are the ones I later see running jobs. Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: if your boss lets you, be there when the inspector walks the rough. Ask what he's looking at. Ask which code edition is in effect for that permit, and then go read the section he wrote up. Bring the permit card and the plans without being asked.

You'll carry material for months no matter what. Spend twenty minutes of it learning what passes and why. It's the cheapest education on the job.

threads.author: haddad_mech
threads.title: From the hiring side: why a paper trail matters more than you think
threads.body:
Here's what I look for when I hire, and it's not what most young guys expect.

When someone tells me they have three years of experience and all of it was cash, I usually believe them. But I can't verify it, and on our public jobs everybody goes on certified payroll from day one, so I'm starting them at zero on paper whether I like it or not.

The applicants who stand out walk in with something I can check: pay stubs or W-2s, a 608 card, a letter from a past employer, a log of jobs with dates and who they worked under. It doesn't have to be fancy. It has to exist.

If you're getting paid cash right now, start that log tonight. Nobody's coming to build it for you later.
fact_risk: certified payroll on public (prevailing-wage) jobs

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: a log you keep yourself helps you remember. A supervisor's signature or a pay stub is something someone else can check. For a license, read what the board actually asks for before you assume either one is enough.

threads.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
threads.title: Boss calls late September 'boiler cleaning month.' What am I actually doing?
threads.body:
About 7 months in at the shop out of Bayonne. Boss says starting next week it's boiler cleanings and fall service every day until it gets cold, mostly old one-pipe steam in Bayonne and JC, some hot water. Ziggy told me to ask for one new thing a week so this is me asking ahead of time.

What actually happens on a fall service for an old steam boiler? What should I be watching so I'm not just the guy holding the light? brother I've seen maybe three steam boilers up close.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Fall service on steam is about making sure January is boring, kid.

Your lead will look at the water line in the gauge glass, check the low-water cutoff and flush it if it's the kind you flush, look at the pressure control and the pigtail under it, check the burner and the flue, and look for leaks on the near-boiler piping. You'll be holding the bucket and the light. Watch the order he does it in and ask why after, not during.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, bring a notebook. Second, write down the make and model of every boiler and what the water looked like in the glass. Third, ask your lead what "normal" is for that one, because every old steam system has its own normal. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: what's a pigtail? sorry. is that the loop thing under the gauge?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: That's the one. It protects the control from live steam. Old ones clog up with crud, which is why we look at them every fall. You'll see.

replies.author: benplumb79

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Is it true you're never supposed to add water to a steam boiler while it's hot? My teacher said that once and I wasn't sure if it was a rule or a saying.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: It's a real rule. Feeding cold water into a hot boiler that's run low can crack it, or worse. That's why we teach people to stop and find out why it's low before anything else. On a fall service your lead handles that, not the helper.

threads.title: Electrical helper here. Boss says we get no-heat calls in winter too?
threads.body:
About a month into my first helper job (residential electrical, Irvington and around). My lead mentioned that once it gets cold we'll get calls from people whose boiler or furnace "has no power," and that half the time it's something electrical.

I assumed no-heat was an HVAC or plumbing call. What are electricians usually finding on these? And where's the line between our job and the heating guy's? I don't want to be the new guy poking at a burner.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly most of them are simple: a service switch somebody turned off, a tripped breaker, a thermostat wire that got chewed or cut during a remodel, a bad transformer feeding the controls. The electrician's job is to prove power is getting where it's supposed to, and stop there if it's the heating side. Test, don't guess, and don't start replacing HVAC parts you weren't called for.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: From the HVAC side, first: tell the homeowner you're there for the electrical, not the boiler. Second, if your side checks out, say so and let them call the heating company. Electricians who start adjusting burner controls make my life harder.

replies.author: hec_does_ac

replies.author: threeway_02

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: That's the line. And when you find the switch at the top of the basement stairs turned off, don't laugh in front of the customer. Laugh in the truck.

threads.author: oldsteam_zig
threads.title: Last week of September: what I want my helpers doing before the phones start
threads.body:
Every year the last week of September is the calm before the phones. Here's what I tell my helpers.

Stock your truck like it's January. Fittings for the old stuff, not just the new stuff. Nipples, unions, gauge glasses, pigtails, a couple of the controls we always end up needing.

Know where every shutoff is on your regular customers' boilers before it's dark at five.

Test your flashlight, your CO meter, your combustion analyzer. Get your boots resoled now, not the first wet week.

And sleep. On-call season is long, kid. The guy who's rested at 2am does better work than the guy who's been up since Tuesday. That's the job.

threads.author: big_hector_plumb
threads.title: CO meter went off before I hit the bottom of the basement stairs
threads.body:
service call in a 4-family in union city, water heater "making a smell." basement door was shut. my CO meter started going off before i got to the bottom of the stairs. flue pipe had come apart at the chimney.

got out, got the tenants out of the first floor, called the gas company from the sidewalk. they shut it down. the super was mad at ME lol.

4 years in and never had my meter go off like that. how many of you actually carry one, and actually turn it on?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Glad you're okay. What you did is the right order: get out, get others out, call the utility or 911 from outside, and don't go back in until it's been cleared. A personal CO meter is PPE, same as your glasses. Bump test or check it the way the manufacturer says, so you know it works when you need it. Different trade, same rule. Stay safe.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: On the bump testing Marcus mentioned: first, follow the manufacturer's calibration and bump-test schedule. It's in the manual and it's not optional. Second, a cheap meter that works beats an expensive one sitting in the truck. Third, if nobody knows when yours was last checked, assume it hasn't been. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: we got ours from the shop this summer... nobody told us anything about bump testing. going to ask monday

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Scary one. My father had a call like that in Harrison years ago. What I'd tell a young guy: if the meter goes off, open it up, let it air out, and once the meter clears, fix the flue and get on with it.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Respectfully, Rui, I wouldn't tell a young guy that. Get out first. Let the gas company or the fire department clear the building and find the source. Then you come back. Airing it out and going back to work is how good mechanics end up in the hospital.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: You're right, Ziggy. I said that wrong. Out first, utility or fire department, then the work. Thanks for catching it.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: once you're allowed back in, make sure the building's CO alarms are there and working. A flue that came apart at the chimney may also mean somebody did work without an inspection. Worth noting on your ticket.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What every one of my techs carries on every call:
- Personal CO meter, on, before entering the basement
- Combustion analyzer on any fuel-burning work
- The gas utility's emergency number saved in the phone
And they're trained to leave first and diagnose second.

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: Felt a tingle in a wet crawlspace in Manville. What do you check before going under a house?
threads.body:
Crawlspace job in Manville last week, replacing a section of drain under an old ranch. There was an inch of water down there from the storms. The work light was on an extension cord plugged into a garage outlet, no GFCI. Halfway through, the light flickered and I felt a tingle in my hand where I was holding the light and kneeling in the water. I got out right away.

The cord had a nick in it. I'm fine. My boss said I should have checked the cord, and he's right, but I also had no idea the garage outlet wasn't GFCI protected.

What do you all do before going into a wet crawlspace? I'd like a routine instead of luck.
fact_risk: GFCI requirements for temporary power
permit-required confined space determination

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
First: you got out. That was the right call. A tingle in a wet space is a warning, not a nuisance.

Before any wet crawlspace: GFCI protection at the source, or a portable GFCI at the plug, and test it every time. Inspect the whole cord, end to end. Use lights rated for damp locations. And if there's standing water and anything electrical involved, the job can wait until it's dry. Stay safe.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: I didn't know portable GFCIs were a thing. Ordering one tonight.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Ground-fault protection for temporary power on a job is a standard requirement, and a garage outlet in an older house may well predate GFCI. Don't assume any outlet in an older house is protected. Test it.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly after Sandy we did hundreds of crawlspaces down here, and that's the one thing I drilled into every helper. Portable GFCI on every cord, every time. Water under a house is a different job.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Crawlspace routine at my company:
- Look before you crawl: water, wiring, animals, smell
- Portable GFCI and a cord you've inspected
- Someone outside who knows you're in there
- Phone or radio on you
- If it smells like sewage or gas, nobody goes in yet

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: 1st year here. Our instructor calls crawlspaces confined spaces 'in spirit.' Not sure that's the official definition, but it stuck with me.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Careful with that one. Whether a space counts as a permit-required confined space is a specific determination, and some crawlspaces could qualify depending on the hazards. On our jobs the competent person makes that call. Your instructor's instinct is right, though: treat it with that respect.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: vo-tech electrical guy here, over-explaining: a nicked cord plus wet ground means you were the path. that's literally what our teacher draws on the board every year. glad you're not the example now

replies.author: benplumb79

That's a sentence I won't forget anytime soon.

replies.author: Dev_H

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: One more: if you ever take a real shock, even if you feel fine afterward, tell someone and consider getting checked out. Some injuries don't show up right away.

replies.author: benplumb79

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Rung cracked on the homeowner's old wooden ladder during my ride-along

threads.author: hec_does_ac
threads.title: Heat wave week: 14 no-cool calls in two days and what I keep telling new techs
threads.body:
So this one time in AC... ok it's this week, not one time lol. 14 no-cool calls Monday and Tuesday between Cherry Hill and Washington Township. Half were dirty filters and clogged condensate lines, a couple capacitors, one frozen coil the homeowner "fixed" by turning the thermostat down to 60.

What I keep telling my new guys on ride-alongs... check airflow before you even think about the charge. Check the condensate before you blame the unit. Drink water in the truck between every call, not when you're already dizzy. And if the attic is an oven, do the attic part first thing in the morning and come down for air often. Nobody gets a medal for passing out over an air handler.

What are you guys seeing this week?

Same here in Middlesex. What I'd add for the new techs:
- Write down what you found, even on the easy calls; patterns show up
- Don't promise same-day on a part you don't have on the truck
- Heat-wave callbacks cost more than the calls did

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Side jobs, from the owner's side: what happens when yours calls my office
threads.body:
Happened again this month, so I'll write it down. A homeowner called us for a no-cool on a mini-split installed last year. Not our install. A helper from another shop put it in on weekends, cash. No permit, no proper evacuation, flare connections leaking. The homeowner wanted to know who to call about it, and the answer was nobody.

What it looks like from my side:
- The homeowner pays twice, once to him and once to us
- If your own boss gets that call, you're probably done there
- Handling refrigerant without your 608 is its own problem, and having the card doesn't make an unpermitted install legal
- You have no insurance, so whatever goes wrong is on you

I'm not telling anyone what to do on their own time. I'm telling you what it costs when it goes wrong.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it. On the electrical side of these, I see the disconnect and the circuit done wrong more than anything else. When unpermitted work turns up later, at a sale or after a problem, the homeowner is usually the one left holding the bill. Check which code edition is in effect and what the town requires before anyone touches a line set.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
And for the no-refrigerant side jobs, like cleaning coils and changing filters for neighbors, it's a smaller exposure but the same basic problem:
- You're still uninsured if you fall off a ladder or break something
- "Just cleaning coils" turns into "while you're here, can you look at this" fast
- Your boss may see it as taking his customers
Ask your boss if the shop wants the maintenance work. Usually they do, and you get the hours.

threads.author: mbell_wireman
threads.title: Prevailing wage vs PLAs: why the big public jobs look the way they do
threads.body:
This keeps coming up, so here's the union-side view. I'd welcome the non-union contractors here to correct me where it's different for them.

Prevailing wage is a floor. On covered public work, everyone gets at least the published rate for their trade and county, union or not.

A project labor agreement is a different thing. It's an agreement for a specific project, usually a big one, about labor terms: hiring through the trades, how disputes get handled, no strikes. You'll hear about them on large public construction.

If you're an apprentice and you land on one of these jobs, a few things will be new: sign-in sheets, long safety orientations, and someone checking that your classification matches your paperwork. Bring your ID, bring your card, wear your glasses. Stay safe.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Where the money from a $189 service call actually goes
threads.body:
Every year a new tech sees an invoice and asks why he makes $22 an hour when we charged $189 for forty minutes. Fair question. Here's roughly how I explain it at my shop. Numbers differ everywhere; this is the shape, not a formula.
- The tech's wage, plus payroll taxes and workers' comp on top of it
- The truck: payment, fuel, insurance, repairs, the stock on the shelves
- The office: the person who answered the phone and scheduled you
- Drive time between calls that the customer never sees on the bill
- Callbacks, which we fix for free
- Slow weeks in October when the phones are quiet and everyone still gets paid
After all that, a healthy shop keeps a margin, and plenty of shops don't. I'd rather you understand this before you go out on your own and price yourself out of business.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
And if you're wondering why every owner says he's broke when there's a margin: some of them are. Two things:
- A lot of owners pay themselves last
- Equipment margins and service margins are very different animals
I'm not saying every owner is honest about it. I'm saying the $189 isn't profit.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Same on the mechanical side. The number new guys never see is unbilled time. Here's what I look for in a tech who's earned a raise: the one whose calls don't come back. A callback is the most expensive hour we have.

Not billed separately in a flat call fee. Different thing from your pay:
- Driving between calls during the workday should be paid to you as hours worked, as far as I know
- If it isn't, that's a conversation with your boss, and the state labor department has the details

threads.author: oldsteam_zig
threads.title: Torch work in old houses: stick around after you put the torch down
threads.body:
Had a helper sweat a couple of fittings on a boiler near a joist bay in Lodi last week. Nice joints. We packed up, I went back down for a tool I forgot, and I smelled it before I saw it. The old wood and the dust up in that bay had been smoldering the whole time.

Nobody got hurt and the house is fine. But here's what everybody on my trucks does now, and what I should have made him do:

Fire cloth behind the joint before you light the torch, not after. Wet down old framing if it's dry as paper. Spray bottle and an extinguisher on the floor next to you, not out on the truck. And when you're done, stay and watch it for half an hour. Put your hand near the wood. Look up into the bay with a light.

Old balloon-frame houses in Bergen have bays that run open floor to floor. A spark goes up there and you won't see it until it's a real problem.

Thirty minutes of watching is cheap. That's the job.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
You got lucky in the right way. A lot of the press fittings on the market now are designed to leak when they haven't been pressed, so you find them under test instead of months later behind drywall. It did its job.

If a fitting is pressed and still leaks, the usual causes on our jobs: the pipe wasn't fully inserted, a burr or a rough cut nicked the O-ring, dirt on the pipe, a dented or out-of-round end, or the wrong jaw for the size. Cut square, deburr, wipe, mark, insert to the mark, press. Every time.

Here's what I look for when I hire, by the way: somebody who marks depth on couplings too.

threads.title: what does a 4-way switch actually do in the middle?
threads.body: UA 1st year, plumbing, so this is pure curiosity. replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly it's simpler than it sounds. Both travelers come into the 4-way, and it either passes them straight through or crosses them over, so whichever way the other switches sit, flipping it changes which traveler is live at the far end. A 3-way can't do that swap, which is why the middle one has to be a 4-way. Draw it: two 3-ways on the ends, the 4-way in the middle, and trace it with your finger in every position.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: One thing to add for when you see these in the field: check the 4-way's instructions for which screws are the pair in and which are the pair out. They aren't always laid out the same, and mixing them up gives you exactly the "works sometimes" complaint.

threads.title: re-identifying the white wire on a switch loop, is tape enough
fact_risk: re-identifying the white conductor in a switch loop, white as the supply (NEC 200.7(C))
neutral at switch locations (NEC 404.2(C)) and when it applies
threads.body: residential remodel in manahawkin. old part of the house has a ceiling light fed at the fixture, with a 2-wire cable down to the switch. my boss wraps black tape on the white at both ends and moves on. in school they mentioned something about needing a neutral at switches now. is the tape enough on an existing loop, and does the newer code mean we have to rewire it when we touch it?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Re-identifying the white with tape or another permanent marking, wherever it's visible and accessible, is the long-standing way to use it as a hot in a switch loop. In a loop the white is supposed to be the supply going to the switch, not the return to the light.

The neutral-at-the-switch requirement applies to switch locations in the code editions that have it, with exceptions. Whether touching an existing loop pulls you into it depends on the edition and the scope of the permit, so check which code edition is in effect and ask your inspector before you assume.

He swapped the old bulbs for LEDs and now with both switches off they glow really faint, like a nightlight. He says it's cheap bulbs and to ignore it. replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: had this in my apartment, swapped brands and it went away. so cheap bulbs, or was something else going on with mine too?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Could be the bulbs, could be the wiring, and it's worth knowing which. The common harmless cause: on a 3-way the two travelers run side by side in the same cable, and on a long run a little voltage couples from one to the other. An incandescent never shows it. An LED needs so little that it glows. Lighted switches do the same thing.

The cause you want to rule out is the switches breaking the neutral instead of the hot. Then the fixture is still hot when it's off, and somebody changing a bulb gets a surprise. Have someone qualified check it with a meter. If it's coupling, a different bulb or a small device made for this usually fixes it. Stay safe.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: how does an AFCI actually tell a bad arc from a light switch?
fact_risk: how combination AFCIs detect series and parallel arcing
threads.body: ok so last year in class we covered AFCIs and the teacher said they detect "dangerous arcing." but every time you flip a switch or plug something in there's a little arc, and a brushed motor like a drill arcs constantly. so how does the breaker know which arc is the bad one? is it just guessing off some pattern? because from what I hear on here they trip on random stuff and miss other stuff, so I'm skeptical. also the teacher couldn't really answer it so here I am

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Good question, and the skepticism is reasonable. In plain terms: the breaker has electronics that watch the current waveform for the signature of a dangerous arc, the erratic high-frequency noise and the pattern a loose or damaged conductor makes over time, as opposed to the brief, predictable arc of a switch or the steady noise of a motor. Combination types look for arcing in series, like a loose connection, and from line to neutral or ground, like damaged insulation. Many also sense ground faults.

It is pattern recognition, so it isn't perfect. Some motors and electronics look suspicious to some models. That's part of why the designs keep getting updated.

replies.body: Plumbing guy, but that was a better explanation than I've gotten from two years of listening to electricians complain about them. Thanks for asking it.

threads.author: plumbguy917
threads.title: New dishwasher trips the GFCI on the dry cycle. On us or the electrician?
fact_risk: GFCI protection for dishwasher outlets (varies by code edition and NYC code)
threads.body:
1st year, Local 1. Last week my journeyman had me do the water and drain on a dishwasher in a Bay Ridge apartment, the electrician did the circuit. Customer called back: it runs through wash and rinse fine, then the GFCI trips on the heated dry. Electrician says it's the appliance. Customer's blaming us because we were the last ones under there lol.

Is there any way a water connection trips a GFCI, or is this not our problem?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: It can absolutely be your problem without being your circuit. A GFCI trips when current leaks to ground. Two common causes on a new dishwasher: the heating element leaking current once it gets hot, which is the appliance, and water getting into the junction box under the front, which can be a weeping supply fitting right above it.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: had a callback like this in cherry hill... the elbow on the supply was weeping onto everything, you couldn't see it unless the kick plate was off and it was running

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly the dry-cycle detail is the clue. Heat makes a failing element leak, and heat plus a little water in a box makes a GFCI unhappy. Look at your fitting first because it's free: dry the whole area, run a cycle with the kick plate off, flashlight on the connection. If it's bone dry and it still trips on heat, it's the appliance and the customer calls the manufacturer. Either way, nobody bypasses the GFCI.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: My uncle tapes the threaded side of the dishwasher elbow (never the compression side) and checks it with a paper towel after the first fill. The paper towel shows drips you can't see.

threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: Sump pumps on GFCI: what I tell homeowners after every big storm
fact_risk: GFCI required for basement receptacles in current NEC editions
removal of the dedicated single-receptacle (sump) exception several code cycles ago
hardwired sump pumps and GFCI rules / local acceptance
threads.body:
Every big rain, I hear the same complaint: "the GFCI tripped and my basement flooded, why does code make me do this?" Here's how I explain it.

Current code editions want GFCI protection on basement receptacles, and the old exception that let a single dedicated sump receptacle skip it went away several cycles back. Check which code edition is in effect for your permit, because an older install may have been legal when it went in.

A GFCI that trips on a sump pump is usually telling you something. Pumps sit in water, and as they age the windings and cords leak current. That leak is exactly the thing that kills people in wet basements.

So the answer I give isn't "remove the GFCI." It's: put a high-water alarm in the pit, think hard about a battery backup pump, test the GFCI and the pump before storm season, and replace a pump that keeps tripping it. Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it after too many flooded basements.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'm torn on this one and I'll say it. After Ida I had three customers with flooded basements, and every one was a tripped GFCI on the sump. I install it the way the code says, but I push the alarm and the backup pump hard, because a GFCI by itself is a bad plan in a basement that floods.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Fair, and we're not that far apart. The GFCI isn't the plan, it's the protection. The alarm and the backup pump are the plan.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Plumber's side: half the pumps I pull that were tripping GFCIs have a cord that's been sitting in water or a motor on its way out. Replace the pump, check the check valve while you're there, and the trips go away. A good pump tripping a good GFCI is rare.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: As a student, may I ask why not put the sump on its own hardwired circuit with no receptacle at all? Wouldn't that avoid the GFCI question entirely?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Good question. Depending on the pump, the code edition and what your local office accepts, hardwiring can change the analysis, but most pumps are cord-and-plug so they can be swapped fast at 2am. Ask the inspector before you plan around it. I wouldn't treat it as a loophole.

threads.author: ms_almonte
threads.title: Target superheat needs indoor wet bulb. Students, buy the probe.
fact_risk: target superheat charts use indoor (return) wet bulb and outdoor dry bulb
threads.body:
Every summer a few of my former students come back from their first jobs saying they "checked the superheat" on a piston system and it was fine. Then I ask what their target was and they look at me.

First, superheat by itself is just a number. On a fixed orifice system you compare it to a target, and the target comes from the manufacturer's chart or a target superheat chart, using indoor wet bulb and outdoor dry bulb.

Second, wet bulb, not dry bulb. Wet bulb tells you how much moisture the coil is dealing with, and that moves the target a lot. A sticky July afternoon in Paterson and a dry day in September want different numbers.

Third, measure the return air at the unit, not in the hallway.

Buy a decent wet bulb probe before you buy the fancy gauges. Ask me how I know which one matters more.

threads.author: HeatwaveOnCall
threads.title: where can a condensate pump actually drain in a finished basement
fact_risk: acceptable condensate disposal points (local plumbing code / inspector)
air gap or air break for indirect waste
condensate pump safety switch wiring
threads.body: ok so long story, we're doing a furnace and coil swap in a split-level in clifton and the basement is getting finished. right now the condensate pump just dumps into the laundry sink with the tube clipped on the edge. homeowner wants it "hidden," so the contractor finishing the basement asked if we can run it into the washer standpipe or tie it into the sump pit. my lead said "depends" (of course) and that it's the inspector's call. what are the normal options and which ones get people in trouble? also does the pump need anything wired to it besides the plug

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First thing my students forget: condensate is waste, and where it goes is a plumbing code question in your town, so the inspector really is the answer. Second: whatever it drains into, don't make a direct connection to a drain without an air gap or air break. You don't want sewer gas coming back up the tube, or a backup pushing into the pump.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Field version, around here:
- Laundry tub, or a standpipe with an air gap, is the common option and usually accepted. Check locally
- The sump pit gets used a lot and some towns don't allow it. Ask before you do it
- Never glue it straight into a drain or a vent with no trap and no air gap
- Wire the pump's safety switch so the AC shuts off if the pump fails. Most pumps have the switch; plenty of installers never connect it
- Leave access. Finished basements bury pumps behind drywall and then it's a callback

The safety switch is the one that saves the new floor.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: update: inspector was fine with the standpipe with an air gap. we wired the safety switch into the furnace control so the ac stops if the pump dies. contractor is building a little access door. thanks everyone

threads.author: hec_does_ac
threads.title: Cape Cods: ductless heads upstairs or a ducted unit in the kneewall?
fact_risk: multi-zone outdoor units powering heads through the interconnect
threads.body:
Settle a fight at my shop... we're doing a lot of Capes in Gloucester and Camden County this summer, upstairs is 85 by 3pm and there's no ductwork up there. Half our guys sell a head in every bedroom. The other half want a small ducted air handler in the kneewall or the attic with short runs to each room.

So this one time in AC I put three heads in a Cape and the customer called the next summer saying the kid's room was freezing and clammy and the other two were fine lol. Oversized head in a tiny room.

What do you guys do and how do you decide? Not looking for a brand war.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
How I decide:
- Small bedrooms: the smallest wall head is often too big for them, so it short-cycles and doesn't pull moisture out. That favors ducted
- Kneewall space: if there's room for an air handler with short, sealed runs and a real return, ducted is quieter and cleaner looking
- If the kneewall is cramped, or the customer wants room-by-room control, heads
- Either way, the insulation in those kneewalls is usually terrible, so price the air sealing in

Margins are better on the ducted job if you price the labor honestly.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's how it plays out for us: the ducted kneewall unit is the better system when there's room, but it takes a tech who can actually design duct. Heads are more forgiving for a crew that's still learning. I sell the system my people can install well.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: we did a cape in clifton with one ducted unit in the attic over the dormer and it was so quiet the customer thought it was off. getting up there in july was brutal though

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly on the raised houses at the shore after Sandy we did a lot of heads, because there was nowhere to put anything. Not Capes, but the same problem: no space, no ducts.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: For the electricians wondering whether one ducted unit means less circuit work: it depends on the setup. A multi-zone outdoor unit usually powers its heads through the interconnect, so that's one circuit to the outdoor unit. Three separate single-zone systems are three circuits. Follow the install manual either way.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: And the question every customer asks, can you hide the linesets without it looking like spaghetti lol... lineset covers, run them on the back of the house, and talk about it before the install, not after. Some people hate the look of a head no matter what. Those are your ducted customers.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Good thread, I'm stealing it for class. What students should take away is that you decide from the house: the room sizes, the space, the insulation, the customer. Not from whatever your shop usually sells.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: Parents' Cape is getting mini-splits. What's the electrician's part?
fact_risk: circuit sizing from nameplate MCA and MOCP
HVAC disconnect within sight of the unit (NEC 440.14)
GFCI for outdoor HVAC equipment (2020 NEC 210.8(F)) and later changes/local amendments
threads.body: my parents' cape in hamilton is getting a 3-zone mini-split next month and the hvac company said "you'll need an electrician for the power." my dad looked at me because I'm in the electrical program at vo-tech, which, no, I'm a student. but I want to understand what the electrician is actually going to do so I can watch and not be useless. like how do they know what size breaker, what's the box on the wall outside for, and does it need a GFCI? our book says something about outdoor GFCI but my teacher said it's complicated

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Your teacher's right that it's complicated. Here's the outline. Wire and breaker size come from the outdoor unit's nameplate: the minimum circuit ampacity sets the wire, the maximum overcurrent protection sets the largest breaker allowed. The box outside is the disconnect, which the code wants within sight of the unit so a tech can kill it while working on it.

The GFCI part: a recent code edition expanded GFCI requirements for outdoor outlets in a way that caught HVAC equipment, a lot of inverter units nuisance tripped, and there were changes and local amendments afterward. Check which code edition is in effect for your parents' permit. That's a question for the inspector, not the internet.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: From the HVAC side, also watch the interconnect between the outdoor unit and the heads. Most multi-zone units power the heads from the outdoor unit through that cable, and the manual specifies the wire. Nobody should be using leftover thermostat wire for it.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: Watch where the condensate from each head goes too. Not electrical, but my uncle got called to a Cape where a head was draining into the wall cavity lol

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Three conversion quotes, three different answers on the chimney
fact_risk: orphaned water heater draft problems / chimney liner sizing
sidewall vent materials per manufacturer
threads.body:
Different kind of question from me. We're finally converting our own house in Piscataway from oil to gas: split-level, oil boiler with baseboard, hot water off a tankless coil in the boiler. Got three quotes and they disagree on the chimney.

Quote 1: new gas boiler and a new gas water heater, both into the chimney with a new liner.
Quote 2: high-efficiency boiler vented out the side wall in plastic, new water heater into the existing chimney, no liner.
Quote 3: high-efficiency boiler out the side wall, a separate sidewall-vented water heater, chimney not used at all.

Quote 2 is cheapest. Quote 1's guy says Quote 2 is going to cause problems. Who's right, and why does the chimney matter so much? Appreciate it. Kash told me to get more than one quote, so here we are. Still doing ride-alongs too, so this is half for the house and half for me.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Quote 1's guy is pointing at a real problem, kid. That old chimney was sized for an oil boiler sending a lot of hot exhaust up it. Take the boiler out, and a gas water heater alone in that big flue is what we call an orphaned water heater. Not enough heat to draft right, so the flue gas cools and condenses, and you get weak draft, moisture eating the masonry, and possibly exhaust spilling into the basement.

That's why conversions get a liner sized for whatever's left in the chimney, or take the chimney out of the picture like Quote 3. Quote 2 could be fine if they actually checked that chimney, so ask them exactly how. If the answer is "it'll be fine," that's a no.

And CO detectors on every floor, whoever you pick.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What I'd ask all three:
- Did you do a heat loss, or are you matching the old boiler's size? Old oil boilers are usually oversized
- Who removes or abandons the oil tank, and is it in the price?
- Who handles the gas service with the utility?
- What's the warranty on the installation, not just the equipment?

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Sorry, newer guy question. Is the side wall vent the white plastic pipe sticking out of the side of houses? I always wondered what those were.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body:
Thanks Ziggy, this is exactly what I needed. Going to ask Quote 2 how they checked the chimney.

edit: Quote 2 said they'd "see when they get there." Going with Quote 3.

threads.author: big_hector_plumb
threads.title: Customer wants the old oil tank left in the basement after the gas conversion
fact_risk: NJ DEP involvement and certified contractors when a heating oil tank leaks
municipal permits for tank removal or abandonment in place
homeowners insurance coverage of tank leaks
NYC rules for cellar/vault oil tanks
threads.body:
Service tech, Union City. Finishing a conversion next week in a two-family in Weehawken. Customer wants the 275 gallon oil tank in the basement just left there, empty, "for later." Then he tells me the home inspector on another house he's buying found a buried tank in the yard during the tank sweep, and the seller says "it was abandoned years ago."

Boss is out till Monday and I'm bad at talking to customers lol. What do I tell him on both? I know we don't do tank work, I just don't want to sound like an idiot.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Basement tank first. Empty is never empty, kid. There's always sludge and some oil in the bottom. Leave it and it leaks someday, or the next buyer's inspector flags it. On most of our conversions the tank comes out: pumped, cleaned, cut up, hauled. Your town may want a permit for the removal. Tell him your boss will price it, and don't let him keep it "for later."

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
On the buried tank, from my experience in NJ:
- Ask the seller for paperwork. "Abandoned" without a permit and closure paperwork from the town means very little
- If there's any sign of a leak, it becomes a cleanup, and in NJ that brings in DEP rules and certified contractors
- His attorney and insurance company should hear about it before closing, not after
- None of this is yours to sort out. Send him to his attorney and a tank company

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: And on the buried one, I'd want it pulled and the soil tested before I bought that house.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Respectfully, Ziggy, pulling isn't always the answer on buried tanks. Some are under a porch, an addition or a driveway, and abandonment in place, done properly with a permit and soil sampling, is what gets done. The paperwork is the thing. Depends on the town.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Fair, Rui. If it can't come out, it's done on paper. My point is "abandoned years ago" with no paper isn't abandoned.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: dumb question, why is a buried tank such a big deal if it's just sitting there? like if it's not leaking what's the problem? and who even checks

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: Because old steel in wet soil eventually leaks, and nobody knows when. When it does, the cleanup can get very expensive, and it can land on the homeowner. That's why buyers here do tank sweeps, and why sellers get nervous about them.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: had one in deptford where the customer's homeowners insurance didn't cover the leak. paid out of pocket. appreciate this thread

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: On who actually does the tank work: mostly a separate company. On our commercial jobs it's always a sub with its own insurance for that work. Here's what I look for in that sub: their permits and paperwork, every time.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Electrical side note: the oil burner circuit and its emergency switch should be removed or properly reused during the conversion. I've seen dead burner switches left at the top of the stairs for decades confusing everybody. Label it or remove it.

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body: talked to him today. basement tank is coming out, boss is pricing it. told him the yard one is a lawyer question. he actually listened lol. thier inspector already told them the same thing so that helped

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: That's how you do it. My father used to say the customer remembers how you said it more than what you said.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: We're in the middle of our own conversion and tank removal was in all three quotes. Reading this, I'm glad it was.
